Testimony on L.D. 851, An Act to Establish a Senior Retiree Lobster License
Presented by Representative Robert A. Foley
District 145
Marine Resources Committee Thursday, March 20, 2025
Good afternoon, Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Marine Resources:
I am State Representative Bob Foley, and I represent the citizens of District 145, which is most of the Town of Wells. I'm here today to introduce my bill, L.D. 851, "An Act to Establish a Senior Retiree Lobster License."
This bill comes to you at the request of one of my constituents -- the Town of Wells Harbor Master, Mike York. The idea stems from a time, many years ago, when Mike had his Maine lobster license back in the mid-1970s. When he joined the service and left Maine, he gave up his lobster license, as he no longer had any ability to utilize it. When he returned to Maine after his time in the service, he entered the workforce and eventually became a harbor master. Mike investigated renewing his lobster license, but at that time, as I understand it, there was a moratorium on new licenses.
As Mike thought about retirement, he thought "lobsterin^' would be something that he, and several others in his same situation, might be able to do to supplement his
income.
The criteria for obtaining a " senior retiree lobster license" is quite restrictive. A person must be at least 65 years of age, be a resident of this state for a minimum of 10 years, and have previously held a commercial lobster and crab fishing license for more than three consecutive years. The individual cannot submerge more than 100 traps, and can only set traps from May 1 through December 1.
This is a limited bill, which will help a retired Mainer, who meets the criteria, earn some supplemental income during their retirement years.
Thank you for your consideration.

District 145 Wells (Part)

TESTIMONY OF Deirdre Gilbert
Department of Marine Resources
The Department of Marine Resources (DMR) is testifying In Opposition to
LD 851 An Act to Establish a Senior Retiree Lobster License Before the Committee on Marine Resources Sponsored by Representative Foley Date of Hearing: March 20, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Marine Resources, my name is Deirdre Gilbert, Director of State Marine Policy for the Department of Marine Resources, and I am testifying on behalf of the Department in opposition to LD 851,
LD 851 would establish a senior retiree lobster and crab fishing license. Such a license would be available only to persons 65 years of age or older who previously held a Class I, II, or III lobster and crab fishing license for at least 3 consecutive years and who have been a Maine resident for at least 10 years. These license holders would be limited to no more than 100 traps, and would only be authorized to fish from May to December.
As you have already heard this session, access to lobster fishing licenses is an ongoing topic of discussion and concern. Lobster is a limited entry fishery, and new entrants must complete the apprenticeship program in order to become eligible for a license. If an individual does not complete the apprenticeship program and meet certain other requirements before reaching the age of 23, then upon completion of the apprenticeship program, they are placed on the waiting list for the Zone in which they apprenticed. New entry is allowed in accordance with the exit ratios established by the Zone Councils. Currently there are 91 individuals on the seven Zone Council waiting lists, some of whom have been waiting as long as 15 years.
Upon reaching the age of 70, an individual who has completed the apprenticeship program becomes automatically eligible for a lobster license and no longer subject to the waiting list. This proposed bill would not require former license holders to have completed the apprenticeship program to re-enter the fishery. The Department's primary concern with the proposed legislation is that there is no way to estimate or account for the new entry that would result, even at a reduced trap limit of 100 traps. For context, in the last 10 years, there have been nearly 1600 commercial lobster and crab fishing licenses not renewed.
Any proposals for new access to this fishery should be considered in light of the specific circumstances the lobster fishery is facing. The overall catch from the lobster fishery has declined 35% from its peak in 2016, and the management trigger developed at ASMFC that was designed to protect the resilience of the stock was tripped in 2023, although the proposed management response (an increase in the minimum gauge) was not implemented due to the industry's objections. DMR is currently conducting

a round of Zone Council meetings to solicit input on alternative approaches to enhance the biological and economic resiliency of the fishery.
In addition, as a result of the still pending federal regulations for the protection of the North Atlantic Right Whale, Maine is likely to face additional management measures to achieve the required risk reduction. In the past, the Take Reduction Team discussed a 400 trap limit for Maine. While that was delayed by the 6-year pause obtained through the Omnibus bill, it remains a very strong likelihood that reduced trap limits will remain a potential management measure coming in 2028. For this reason, DMR is concerned with any proposals that would increase the amount of gear in the fishery.
Thank you for your consideration, and I would be happy to answer any questions you might have.

Against
LD 851 An Act to Establish a Senior Retiree Lobster License
March 20, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Marine Resources Committee, my name is Jarod Bray. I am the Board Chairman of the Maine Lobstermen's Association (MLA). The MLA opposes LD 851 to establish retiree lobster license.
As I testified earlier in March, the MLA is a strong advocate for the zone council process because this system gives lobstermen a voice in local management, working in partnership with the Department of Marine Resources (DMR) and the Legislature. Each zone council has invested significant time in controlling effort in their zone.
This is necessary to ensure Maine does not increase its risk to right whales by putting more gear in the water, that fishery does not have more fishing power than the lobster resource can sustain, and ensure that those who are currently lobstering can remain profitable. New federal whale rules will be in place by the end of 2028. Protecting the resource and keeping existing lobstermen whole are becoming more challenging as lobster landings decline.
LD 851 would allow individuals who do not currently hold a Maine lobster license to obtain a retiree license and fish 100 traps. This proposal both undermines the entry program in place in each of the lobster zones and is extremely unfair to all those who are currently in the Apprentice Program, or have completed the Apprentice Program and are now on a zone waiting list until the required number of licenses have been retired.
Unlike many commercial fisheries, there is a path of entry into the Maine lobster fishery. It requires a commitment to learn the fishery and the importance of our conservation program through the Apprentice Program. And for many, it also requires the person to wait to obtain the privilege to fish in order to limit the overall effort in the fishery depending on which zone they plan to fish in. There are many lobstermen who have given up their lobster license over the years and have had to go through the Apprentice Program to get back into the fishery.
The MLA urges you to vote ought not to pass.
Thank you for your consideration.
